name: Choose Region based on both business requirements and sustainability goals
guideline: Choose a Region for your workload based on both your business requirements and sustainability goals to optimize its KPIs, including performance, cost, and carbon footprint.
context: AWS’s concrete implementation advice: shortlist regions on compliance/cost/latency first, then prefer ones near Amazon renewable-energy projects or with a lower published grid carbon intensity, tracked using the Greenhouse Gas Protocol’s market- or location-based methods.

name: Scale workload infrastructure dynamically
guideline: Use elasticity of the cloud and scale your infrastructure dynamically to match supply of cloud resources to demand and avoid overprovisioned capacity in your workload.
context: AWS lists three concrete approaches — target-tracking (react to a live metric), predictive scaling (anticipate daily/weekly patterns), and schedule-based scaling — and calls out leaving increased capacity running after a demand spike ends as the anti-pattern this guideline is meant to prevent.

name: Align SLAs with sustainability goals
guideline: Review and optimize workload service-level agreements (SLA) based on your sustainability goals to minimize the resources required to support your workload while continuing to meet business needs.
context: AWS frames this as a three-way trade-off: workloads that are highly available, high-performing, or overly secure all tend to consume more resources, and the guidance is explicit that prioritizing any two of those usually costs something on the third — including sustainability.

name:
Stop the creation and maintenance of unused
  assets
guideline: Decommission unused assets in your workload to reduce the number of cloud resources required to support your demand and minimize waste.
context: AWS’s examples of what to look for are concrete: pre-compiled reports, stale datasets, and static images are common candidates, and it points at automatable tools like S3 Lifecycle rules or Data Lifecycle Manager for EBS snapshots rather than manual cleanup.

name: Optimize geographic placement of workloads based on their networking requirements
guideline: Select cloud location and services for your workload that reduce the distance network traffic must travel and decrease the total network resources required to support your workload.
context: AWS’s concrete mechanisms here are caching (CloudFront, ElastiCache) and edge compute (Lambda@Edge) to keep processing physically close to users, plus replacing pre-provisioned static network capacity with shared dynamic capacity so the sustainability cost of that capacity is spread across other subscribers too.

name:
Optimize team member resources for activities
  performed
guideline: Optimize resources provided to team members to minimize the environmental sustainability impact while supporting their needs.
context: AWS’s implementation steps are concrete: energy-efficient workstations with low-power modes, virtual desktops/application streaming to limit hardware upgrade needs, and remote-collaboration tools specifically framed as cutting travel-related emissions, not just convenience.

name: Implement buffering or throttling to flatten the demand curve
guideline: Buffering and throttling flatten the demand curve and reduce the provisioned capacity required for your workload.
context: AWS’s key point: the resources actually consumed track the provisioned-capacity line (sized for the peaks), not the demand curve itself — so flattening peaks via throttling (for clients that can retry) or buffering through a queue/stream like SQS or Kinesis (for clients that can’t) directly cuts provisioned capacity, not just handles overflow.

name:
Optimize software and architecture for asynchronous
  and scheduled jobs
guideline: Use efficient software and architecture patterns such as queue-driven to maintain consistent high utilization of deployed resources.
context: AWS splits this into two concrete mechanisms depending on the job type: queue-driven processing (e.g. AWS Batch job queues, or SQS paired with EC2 Spot Instances) for work that doesn’t need a synchronous response, and scheduling (e.g. EventBridge Scheduler) for work that can run anytime and benefits from being batched.

name:
Remove or refactor workload components with low or
  no use
guideline: Remove components that are unused and no longer required, and refactor components with little utilization to minimize waste in your workload.
context: AWS’s concrete signal for when to act: a significant drop in a Lambda function’s run time can indicate its memory allocation should be lowered, and its consolidation example is running several small databases on one RDS instance rather than each on its own underutilized instance.

name:
Optimize areas of code that consume the most time or
  resources
guideline: Optimize your code that runs within different components of your architecture to minimize resource usage while maximizing performance.
context: AWS’s concrete tooling recommendation is a profiler (Amazon CodeGuru Profiler) to identify which specific code paths are actually consuming the most time or resources, rather than guessing — it even frames this directly as a carbon-footprint reduction technique, not just a performance one.

name:
Optimize impact on devices and
  equipment
guideline: Understand the devices and equipment used in your architecture and use strategies to reduce their usage. This can minimize the overall environmental impact of your cloud workload.
context: AWS’s concrete techniques here include keeping new features backward-compatible (so devices don’t need replacing), moving computationally intense work like image rendering server-side to extend the life of older client devices, and using over-the-air updates so devices don’t need manual servicing.

name:
Use software patterns and architectures that best
  support data access and storage patterns
guideline: Understand how data is used within your workload, consumed by your users, transferred, and stored. Use software patterns and architectures that best support data access and storage to minimize the compute, networking, and storage resources required to support the workload.
context: AWS breaks this down into four concrete characteristics to evaluate per dataset — type (structured/unstructured), growth pattern (bounded/unbounded), durability (persistent/ephemeral/transient), and access pattern (spiky vs. consistent reads/writes) — since the right storage/architecture choice depends on which combination applies.

name: Implement a data classification policy
guideline: Classify data to understand its criticality to business outcomes and choose the right energy-efficient storage tier to store the data.
context: AWS’s process is specific: inventory your data types, group them by criticality/confidentiality/integrity/availability risk, define a classification level and handling policy per group, tag data accordingly, and periodically audit for anything that’s slipped through untagged.

name:
Use technologies that support data access and
  storage patterns
guideline: Use storage technologies that best support how your data is accessed and stored to minimize the resources provisioned while supporting your workload.
context: AWS maps this to concrete technology choices: object storage (S3) for unlimited-scale unstructured data, block storage (EBS) for transactional IOPS-intensive workloads, and purpose-built databases (relational for ACID transactions, key-value like DynamoDB for high-traffic lookup patterns) — the point being no single storage type fits every access pattern.

name: Use policies to manage the lifecycle of your datasets
guideline: Manage the lifecycle of all of your data and automatically enforce deletion to minimize the total storage required for your workload.
context: AWS points at specific automation for this rather than manual review: S3 Lifecycle rules (or S3 Intelligent-Tiering when access patterns are unpredictable), Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager for EBS snapshot/AMI cleanup, and ECR lifecycle policies for expiring old container images by age or count.

name: Use elasticity and automation to expand block storage or file system
guideline: Use elasticity and automation to expand block storage or file system as data grows to minimize the total provisioned storage.
context: AWS’s concrete mechanism is EBS Elastic Volumes, which can change a volume’s size, type, or performance live rather than requiring a pre-sized volume; it also suggests migrating data to object storage entirely where fixed block-volume sizing would otherwise force overprovisioning.

name: Remove unneeded or redundant data
guideline: Remove unneeded or redundant data to minimize the storage resources required to store your datasets.
context: AWS’s anti-pattern list is specific: duplicating data that could just be recreated on demand, backing up everything regardless of actual criticality, and turning on S3 versioning without a business reason for it — all treated as avoidable storage growth, not just “more data than needed.”

name:
Use shared file systems or storage to access
  common data
guideline: Adopt shared file systems or storage to avoid data duplication and allow for more efficient infrastructure for your workload.
context: AWS’s specific recommendation beyond just “use shared storage” is to fetch only the subset of data actually needed for a given job (e.g. an FSx for Lustre file system backed by S3, loading data on demand) and to detach volumes from clients that are no longer actively using them.

name: Minimize data movement across networks
guideline: Use shared file systems or object storage to access common data and minimize the total networking resources required to support data movement for your workload.
context: AWS’s concrete techniques: use compact file formats like Parquet or ORC and compress data before moving it, trim API responses down to only the fields actually needed rather than full records, and aggregate data before transfer wherever record-level detail isn’t actually required.

name: Back up data only when difficult to recreate
guideline: Avoid backing up data that has no business value to minimize storage resources requirements for your workload.
context: AWS ties the backup decision to recovery objectives (RTO/RPO) rather than a blanket policy, and specifically calls out excluding data that’s easy to recreate, ephemeral data, and local copies — unless restoring from a shared location would actually be too slow to meet your SLA.

name:
Use the minimum amount of hardware to meet your
  needs
guideline: Use the minimum amount of hardware for your workload to efficiently meet your business needs.
context: AWS frames this as rightsizing: continuously monitor utilization and use tools like AWS Compute Optimizer or Auto Scaling to match capacity to actual demand, rather than provisioning for peak load year-round.

name: Use instance types with the least impact
guideline: Continually monitor and use new instance types to take advantage of energy efficiency improvements.
context: AWS’s guidance points at specific energy-efficient hardware choices — e.g. migrating to AWS Graviton processors or workload-specific chips like Trainium/Inferentia — and re-evaluating instance types regularly as more efficient ones become available, rather than treating an instance choice as permanent.

name: Use managed services
guideline: Use managed services to operate more efficiently in the cloud.
context: AWS’s own Well-Architected guidance ties this to the "Hardware and services" pillar: prefer managed/serverless offerings over self-managed infrastructure, since the provider can pool and optimize hardware utilization across many customers rather than each workload over-provisioning its own capacity.

name: Optimize your use of hardware-based compute accelerators
guideline: Optimize your use of accelerated computing instances to reduce the physical infrastructure demands of your workload.
context: AWS’s concrete recommendation is to prefer purpose-built accelerator chips over general-purpose GPUs where they fit — it cites AWS Inferentia as offering up to 50% better performance-per-watt than comparable EC2 instances — and to automate decommissioning these instances the moment a job finishes, since idle accelerated hardware is a bigger waste than idle general compute.

name: Communicate and cascade your sustainability goals
guideline: IT teams should clearly understand the organization's sustainability targets and work to communicate and cascade those priorities across its operations.
context: AWS’s practical starting point: since carbon-tracking tooling can be a heavy lift to stand up, use cost as a proxy metric for resource usage in the meantime — it’s a number every team already understands — while tools like the AWS Customer Carbon Footprint Tool track the more direct carbon figure.

name:
Adopt methods that can rapidly introduce
  sustainability improvements
guideline: Adopt methods and processes to validate potential improvements, minimize testing costs, and deliver small improvements.
context: AWS’s concrete approach: test potential improvements against a minimum viable representative set of components rather than the full production system (to keep the cost of testing itself low), and add sustainability requirements to the same development backlog as any other requirement rather than treating them as a separate initiative.

name: Keep your workload up-to-date
guideline: Keep your workload up-to-date to adopt efficient features, remove issues, and improve the overall efficiency of your workload.
context: AWS notes a secondary reason to keep software current beyond efficiency gains: updated versions often ship better tools for measuring your own sustainability impact too, since vendors are chasing their own sustainability goals — and it points at Systems Manager Inventory to find what’s outdated and Patch Manager to automate the update itself.

name: Increase utilization of build environments
guideline: Increase the utilization of resources to develop, test, and build your workloads.
context: AWS’s guidance targets development/test environments specifically: use automation to spin them up only during active working hours and scale them with burstable or spot capacity, rather than running full-size environments idle around the clock.

name: Use managed device farms for testing
guideline: Use managed device farms to efficiently test a new feature on a representative set of hardware.
context: AWS points at services like AWS Device Farm as the concrete example: testing on a shared, managed pool of physical devices avoids each team buying and maintaining its own hardware lab, including older devices that would otherwise go straight to unnecessary upgrades.

name: Use circuit breaker patterns to stop repeated failing operations
guideline: Apply circuit breaker patterns to halt repeated failing operations, preventing unnecessary compute consumption during dependency failures.
context: Azure's own illustration of the waste this prevents: a temporary database outage where application instances keep retrying the failed call while queues grow behind it — the workload can end up consuming far more resources during that recovery period than it did during normal operation.

name: Implement request throttling during overload conditions
guideline: Throttle requests during overload conditions to reduce cascading traffic amplification and backend stress.
context: This is framed as the second line of defense in Azure's failure-amplification scenario: once a circuit breaker stops the retries against a failing dependency, throttling is what keeps the surviving traffic from itself cascading into a backend overload.

name: Use graceful degradation patterns where possible
guideline: Apply graceful degradation so the system maintains partial functionality without triggering excessive recovery behavior.
context: The alternative Azure contrasts this with is a system that either works fully or fails completely — graceful degradation sits in between, keeping partial functionality running rather than triggering the kind of full recovery cycle that consumes disproportionate resources for a partial outage.

name: Detect failure patterns early with monitoring and alerting
guideline: Detect failure patterns early through monitoring and alerting to reduce prolonged inefficient operation and speed recovery.
context: The framing here is about duration, not just detection: catching a failure pattern early is what keeps a workload from sitting in an inefficient, resource-churning state for longer than necessary while nobody notices.

name: Design workloads to isolate dependency failures
guideline: Design workloads so dependency failures are isolated, preventing localized issues from propagating across the system.
context: This is the structural guideline for preventing the failure-amplification pattern described elsewhere in this source in the first place: if one dependency's failure can't propagate, none of the retry storms, queue buildup, or cascading recovery activity described there has a path to occur.

name: Align resiliency architecture to defined business continuity requirements
guideline: Align resiliency architecture with actual business continuity requirements to avoid unnecessary always-on infrastructure and idle redundancy.
context: Azure's specific anti-pattern example: deploying active-active infrastructure across multiple regions for a workload with only modest recovery requirements, which permanently doubles compute and replication overhead even though failover events are rare.

name: Evaluate whether multi-region deployments are truly required
guideline: Evaluate whether multi-region deployments are truly necessary, since unneeded ones add continuous replication traffic and duplicated infrastructure.
context: This is a direct extension of the active-active example given elsewhere in this source — questioning whether the second region is actually required before committing to it, rather than defaulting to multi-region because it's the more resilient-sounding choice.

name: Assess monolith versus microservice tradeoffs carefully
guideline: Carefully weigh monolith versus microservice tradeoffs to avoid unnecessary service-to-service traffic and platform duplication.
context: Azure frames this specifically as a sustainability tradeoff, not just an architectural preference: microservice decomposition that isn't matched by real scaling or isolation needs adds service-to-service network traffic and platform duplication that a monolith wouldn't carry.

name: Right-size failover environments instead of mirroring peak production scale
guideline: Right-size failover environments rather than mirroring peak production scale, minimizing standby infrastructure while still meeting recovery objectives.
context: The contrast Azure draws: a failover environment mirrored at full peak-production scale sits mostly idle except during the rare actual failover, so right-sizing it to what's actually needed to meet recovery objectives — not a 1:1 mirror — is what removes that standing waste.

name: Regularly review backup, replication, and retention strategies
guideline: Regularly review backup, replication, and retention strategies to reduce excessive data duplication and long-term storage growth.
context: This is meant as a recurring practice, not a one-time setup decision: backup, replication, and retention settings tend to be configured once early on and then left unexamined even as the workload's actual recovery needs and data volume change over time.

name: Use asynchronous processing for burst-prone operations
guideline: Use asynchronous processing for burst-prone operations to smooth workload demand and reduce short-lived scale spikes.
context: Azure's concrete illustration is a video processing platform with upload spikes at specific hours — without workload shaping, it scales up rapidly to absorb the burst and then sits substantially idle once demand subsides, which async processing and queuing are meant to smooth out.

name: Implement buffering and queue-based workload management
guideline: Implement buffering and queue-based workload management to stabilize infrastructure utilization over time.
context: This is the specific mechanism behind the video-processing example elsewhere in this source: queue-based buffering lets uploads get processed more steadily over time rather than provisioning enough capacity to absorb the peak the moment it arrives.

name: Batch non-urgent operations where appropriate
guideline: Batch non-urgent operations where appropriate to improve compute efficiency by cutting repeated processing overhead.
context: Distinct from buffering incoming requests (a related guideline): this is about deliberately grouping already-accepted, non-urgent work into batches, since processing many small operations individually carries more repeated overhead than processing the same total work in fewer, larger passes.

name: Tune autoscaling policies to avoid aggressive short-term scaling reactions
guideline: Tune autoscaling policies to avoid aggressive short-term scaling reactions that expand infrastructure unnecessarily during temporary spikes.
context: Azure names this specifically as a tradeoff to manage carefully: autoscaling genuinely improves utilization, but a policy tuned to react too aggressively to short-term spikes can itself create unnecessary infrastructure churn — scaling up and back down repeatedly costs more than a smoother, better-tuned response would.

name: Evaluate managed PaaS and serverless services where appropriate
guideline: Evaluate managed PaaS and serverless services where appropriate to improve infrastructure utilization through shared platform efficiency and reduce operational overhead.
context: The efficiency case Azure makes: managed PaaS and serverless platforms make better use of shared cloud infrastructure than self-managed dedicated resources, and they also benefit automatically from Microsoft's own ongoing platform-level efficiency improvements over time.

name: Keep platform services, runtimes, and dependencies updated
guideline: Keep platform services, runtimes, and dependencies up to date to benefit from ongoing platform efficiency and reliability improvements.
context: This compounds with the PaaS/serverless guideline elsewhere in this source: staying current is specifically what lets a workload keep benefiting from Microsoft's ongoing platform efficiency improvements, rather than being stuck running against an older, less efficient version of the underlying service.

name: Match service tiers and scalability models to actual workload demand
guideline: Match service tiers and scalability models to actual workload demand to prevent overprovisioning and idle infrastructure.
context: Azure frames oversized or underused service tiers as a source of overprovisioning that persists quietly — a tier chosen once at launch based on anticipated demand often stays fixed long after actual usage patterns would justify something smaller.

name: Remove zombie workloads, orphaned resources, and inactive environments regularly
guideline: Regularly remove zombie workloads, orphaned resources, and inactive environments that consume resources without delivering business value.
context: Azure's specific framing: these are resources that continue consuming energy and cost without delivering any business value at all — not underused, but genuinely abandoned — which is why removing them is treated as close to a pure win with minimal tradeoff.

name: Shut down non-production environments when not in use
guideline: Shut down non-production environments when they're not in use to reduce unnecessary compute consumption and idle platform capacity.
context: This targets a specific, common blind spot: non-production environments that were sized like production for convenience and then left running around the clock, even though their actual usage is concentrated in working hours.

name: Avoid dedicated infrastructure allocations unless workload requirements justify them
guideline: Avoid dedicated infrastructure allocations unless workload requirements truly justify them, maximizing use of shared hyperscale infrastructure.
context: Azure's framing is about maximizing use of shared hyperscale infrastructure specifically — dedicated, reserved capacity trades away the efficiency benefit of a shared platform's pooled utilization, so it's positioned as something that needs a genuine requirement behind it, not a default choice.

name: Tune autoscaling behavior to avoid aggressive short-term scaling reactions
guideline: Tune autoscaling behavior to avoid aggressive short-term scaling reactions, stabilizing utilization and reducing unnecessary scale churn.
context: This guideline appears twice in Azure's own framework — once under demand stabilization and again here under platform choices — which is itself a signal of how central avoiding autoscaling churn is to the overall sustainability picture Azure is describing, not a redundant restatement by accident.

name: Use Spot VMs only for interrupt-tolerant workloads
guideline: Use Spot VMs only for interrupt-tolerant workloads to improve infrastructure utilization without introducing avoidable reliability instability.
context: Azure's explicit tradeoff: Spot VMs improve infrastructure utilization by using otherwise-idle capacity, but that capacity can be reclaimed with little notice, so the guideline is specifically scoped to workloads that can tolerate an interruption without it becoming a reliability incident.

name: Choose regions close to users when latency affects workload reliability
guideline: Choose regions close to users when latency affects workload reliability, reducing network traversal overhead and improving request stability.
context: Azure ties this specifically to reliability, not just performance: reduced network traversal doesn't just lower latency, it also reduces the surface area for transient network issues that could otherwise trigger retries and the failure-amplification pattern described elsewhere in this source.

name: Evaluate carbon intensity, latency, and resiliency tradeoffs together when selecting deployment regions
guideline: Weigh carbon intensity, latency, and resiliency together when selecting deployment regions to balance sustainability with reliability and user experience.
context: Azure names this as an explicit tradeoff rather than a simple optimization: a lower-carbon region might increase latency for users, so the recommendation is to weigh all three factors together deliberately rather than optimizing purely for carbon intensity in isolation.

name: Use load testing and chaos engineering to assess how the workload behaves under outages, traffic spikes, and traffic dips
guideline: Use load testing and chaos engineering to see how the workload behaves under outages and traffic spikes or dips, improving resilience and reducing waste during real failures.
context: Azure frames these testing practices as valuable specifically because workloads behave differently under real-world stress than they do in normal operation — the point is exposing reliability issues before they reach production, not testing for its own sake.

name: Use chaos engineering to simulate conditions that increase energy usage and identify inefficient execution paths
guideline: Use chaos engineering to simulate conditions that raise energy usage, exposing inefficient execution paths and supporting resource optimization under stress.
context: This is a distinct use of chaos engineering from the general resiliency-testing guideline elsewhere in this source: here the simulated failure conditions are chosen specifically to surface which execution paths become energy-inefficient under stress, not just which ones break.

name: Define expected system behavior under constrained or inefficient operating conditions
guideline: Define how the system should behave under stress or constrained conditions to ensure predictable recovery and avoid prolonged inefficient operating states.
context: This is what turns chaos-engineering findings into an actual design decision: without a defined expected behavior for degraded conditions, a workload might recover unpredictably or linger in an inefficient operating state longer than necessary after a stress test reveals the weakness.

name: Consider implementing an eco version of the application that reduces features or performance to minimize energy usage
guideline: Consider building a reduced-feature "eco version" of the application as a benchmark for measuring and continuously optimizing energy usage.
context: Azure's specific suggestion is to use this reduced-feature version as a benchmark for sustainability scoring — not necessarily something you'd run in production, but a reference point that makes "how much more efficient could this be" a measurable question rather than a hypothetical one.

name: Evaluate the tradeoff of running chaos engineering and load tests, since these activities themselves consume additional compute and increase emissions
guideline: Weigh the resource cost of chaos engineering and load testing against their benefits, since testing itself consumes compute and adds emissions.
context: Azure is explicit that this is a real cost, not a hypothetical one: chaos engineering and load testing consume compute and generate emissions just like any other workload, so the value of what a given test round reveals has to be weighed against that footprint.

name: Schedule and scope chaos engineering intentionally to balance resilience validation with the environmental cost of testing
guideline: Schedule and scope chaos engineering intentionally to balance resilience validation against the environmental cost of running tests.
context: This is the practical response to the testing-cost tradeoff named elsewhere in this source: rather than running continuous or excessive chaos testing, scope and schedule it deliberately so the resilience validation gained is proportionate to the environmental cost of running it.

name: Block malicious traffic as early as possible by using edge or network-level controls
guideline: Block malicious traffic as early as possible with edge or network-level controls to reduce compute and network usage from unwanted requests.
context: Azure's concrete illustration: a DDoS attack forcing a system to process large volumes of unwanted requests can trigger autoscaling, higher network throughput, and excessive logging — even if the system stays available throughout, it can end up consuming far more resources than it would under normal operation.

name: Use rate limiting and throttling to control excessive or abusive request patterns
guideline: Apply rate limiting and throttling to control abusive request patterns, preventing workload overload and unnecessary scaling events.
context: This complements blocking malicious traffic outright: rate limiting specifically targets patterns that are abusive or excessive without necessarily being identifiably malicious, which is what would otherwise slip past a pure block-list approach and still trigger unnecessary scaling.

name: Apply identity-based access controls to restrict unauthorized usage
guideline: Apply identity-based access controls to restrict unauthorized usage and reduce processing of invalid or malicious requests.
context: This targets unauthorized rather than malicious traffic specifically — requests that are technically valid in form but shouldn't be allowed at all, which still cost compute to process and reject if they aren't stopped at the identity layer first.

name: Design security layers to filter traffic early rather than at application level
guideline: Design security layers to filter traffic early rather than at the application level, minimizing downstream resource consumption.
context: Azure's explicit tradeoff on this whole section: security isn't free, and adding more inspection layers or routing hops can itself increase processing overhead — the point of filtering as early as possible is to stop unwanted work before it reaches the more expensive, deeper layers of the application.

name: Avoid excessive overlapping security layers unless required
guideline: Avoid excessive overlapping security layers unless truly required, to reduce redundant processing and infrastructure overhead.
context: This is the direct counterpart to the tradeoff Azure names elsewhere in this source: if overdesigned, the security architecture itself becomes a source of extra resource consumption and complexity, so the goal is stopping malicious activity early without stacking redundant inspection on top of it.

name: Harden networking components to reduce exposure and filter unwanted traffic early
guideline: Harden networking components to reduce exposure and filter unwanted traffic early, lowering network and compute usage from malicious requests.
context: Azure frames hardening broadly as inefficiency-reduction, not just risk-reduction: a weakly secured network component tends to attract scanning activity and abnormal traffic patterns that themselves consume resources, independent of whether an attack ever actually succeeds.

name: Harden identity and access controls to ensure only legitimate usage patterns are allowed
guideline: Harden identity and access controls so only legitimate usage is allowed, reducing wasted processing from unauthorized activity.
context: The specific waste Azure calls out: unauthorized or abusive activity that a weak identity layer lets through still gets processed by the application, consuming resources for requests that should never have been accepted in the first place.

name: Harden cloud resource configurations to eliminate weak points and misconfigurations
guideline: Harden cloud resource configurations to eliminate weak points and misconfigurations, preventing exploitation-driven workload spikes.
context: Azure's framing: misconfigurations don't just create risk, they actively invite exploitation attempts and scanning activity that generate real, measurable resource consumption even before (or absent) an actual successful compromise.

name: Harden application and code assets to prevent vulnerabilities from being exploited
guideline: Harden application and code assets to prevent exploited vulnerabilities from causing resource-heavy attack patterns and unstable execution.
context: This targets the specific case where an exploited vulnerability leads to resource-heavy attack patterns or unstable execution — hardening the code itself is what prevents the vulnerability from being usable as an entry point for that kind of resource abuse.

name: Harden operational and management access paths to reduce administrative misuse or accidental impact
guideline: Harden operational and management access paths to reduce administrative misuse or accidental impact, improving stability and reducing unnecessary operational load.
context: This is about the administrative surface specifically, distinct from the application-facing hardening covered elsewhere in this source — misuse or accidental impact through operational access paths can trigger remediation workflows and instability that cost resources just like an external attack would.

name: Filter logs before ingestion into SIEM systems
guideline: Filter logs before they're ingested into SIEM systems to reduce unnecessary data processing, storage, and network transfer.
context: Azure's framing is that security monitoring itself can become a hidden source of waste: forwarding everything to a centralized SIEM without filtering at the source adds processing layers and results in large volumes of stored telemetry that may never actually get used.

name: Collect only security signals required for detection and analysis
guideline: Collect only the security signals required for detection and analysis to minimize telemetry volume and avoid processing unused data.
context: This is the principle behind filtering logs before SIEM ingestion (a related guideline): deciding what's actually needed for detection and analysis upfront, rather than collecting broadly and filtering downstream after the storage and processing cost is already paid.

name: Use cloud-native data collection rules to control and refine telemetry intake
guideline: Use cloud-native data collection rules to control and refine telemetry intake, preventing over-collection and continuous ingestion overhead.
context: Azure's concrete mechanism for controlling telemetry intake at the source, before it accumulates into the over-collection problem described elsewhere in this source, rather than relying on downstream filtering after data has already been ingested and stored.

name: Avoid forwarding full raw datasets when aggregated or filtered signals are sufficient
guideline: Avoid forwarding full raw datasets when aggregated or filtered signals suffice, reducing cross-system data movement and resource use.
context: The specific waste this avoids: moving a complete raw dataset across systems or regions when an aggregated or filtered version would answer the same security question, since that unnecessary data movement carries its own network and processing cost.

name: Design security monitoring pipelines with purpose, not full-fidelity collection by default
guideline: Design security monitoring pipelines with a clear purpose rather than collecting full-fidelity data by default, lowering compute and storage demand while keeping required visibility.
context: This is the overarching principle the previous few guidelines in this source all implement: designing what a security monitoring pipeline collects around an actual detection purpose, rather than defaulting to full-fidelity collection and figuring out later what's actually needed.

name: Apply security controls closer to the source of traffic instead of relying on centralized inspection paths
guideline: Apply security controls closer to the traffic source instead of relying solely on centralized inspection paths, reducing unnecessary network traversal.
context: Azure's framing: centralized inspection increases the distance data has to travel and adds processing at intermediate points, so applying controls closer to where traffic originates avoids that added network traversal in the first place.

name: Avoid hub-and-spoke routing for traffic that does not require centralized inspection
guideline: Avoid hub-and-spoke routing for traffic that doesn't need centralized inspection, minimizing repeated data movement across network layers and regions.
context: This is the concrete architecture this section is arguing against by default: hub-and-spoke routing genuinely improves centralized visibility and control, but for traffic that doesn't actually need centralized inspection, it adds real network overhead without a matching security benefit.

name: Use cloud-native security services that enable local analysis and enforcement
guideline: Use cloud-native security services that enable local analysis and enforcement, reducing cross-system data transfer and improving network efficiency.
context: This is the practical alternative to hub-and-spoke routing named elsewhere in this source: services that can analyze and enforce policy locally avoid the cross-system data transfer that centralized inspection paths require.

name: Design traffic flows to minimize intermediate hops introduced purely for security inspection
guideline: Design traffic flows to minimize intermediate hops added purely for security inspection, lowering bandwidth use and overall infrastructure load.
context: Azure notes this compounds at scale: each additional hop added purely for security inspection increases bandwidth usage and processing load a little on its own, but as traffic volume grows, those small additions compound into meaningfully higher system-wide overhead.

name: Track cost at the feature or workload level, not only at the infrastructure level
guideline: Track cost at the feature or workload level, not just infrastructure, to make hidden inefficiencies easier to find and address.
context: Azure's framing: cost is typically tracked at the infrastructure level while waste actually gets introduced by feature, workflow, and product decisions — that mismatch is what makes real sources of inefficiency hard to find without this finer-grained tracking.

name: Use cost signals as one input to sustainability measurement
guideline: Use cost signals as one input to sustainability measurement, creating a practical basis for tracking improvement over time.
context: Cost is positioned here as a practical proxy, not a perfect one: it's a signal that's already tracked everywhere and correlates with resource consumption, giving teams a usable starting point for sustainability measurement even before dedicated carbon tooling is in place.

name: Define explicit efficiency baselines for critical systems
guideline: Define explicit efficiency baselines for critical systems to help teams detect drift before wasteful patterns become normal.
context: The purpose Azure names specifically: a defined baseline is what lets a team notice drift — a system slowly becoming less efficient over time — before that gradual change gets normalized as just how the system behaves.

name: Treat observability spend as part of the optimization scope
guideline: Treat observability spend as part of the optimization scope to limit logging and telemetry growth that adds cost without enough value.
context: Azure calls this out as a specific blind spot: logging, metrics, and tracing are valuable, but treated as free they can grow into their own significant source of ongoing compute, storage, and ingestion cost that nobody is actively managing.

name: Assign cost accountability at the workload level
guideline: Assign cost accountability at the workload level to encourage end-to-end optimization instead of isolated local fixes.
context: This is what closes the loop on tracking cost at the feature/workload level (a related guideline): visibility alone doesn't drive optimization if nobody is actually accountable for the number once it's visible.

name: Challenge local optimizations that shift cost elsewhere
guideline: Challenge local optimizations that merely shift cost elsewhere, improving system-wide efficiency rather than moving waste between teams.
context: Azure's specific concern: without clear ownership boundaries, a team can genuinely improve their own component's metrics while simply moving the underlying inefficiency somewhere else in the workload rather than actually eliminating it.

name: Reduce API chattiness, payload size, and unnecessary repeat calls
guideline: Reduce API chattiness, payload size, and unnecessary repeat calls to lower avoidable compute demand and network transfer.
context: Azure's illustrative anti-pattern: a system built around heavy microservice decomposition and chatty APIs that works fine initially, but where an increasing share of cost comes from inter-service communication and redundant data movement rather than the actual business logic as usage grows.

name: Prioritize algorithm and execution-path improvements in code that dominates runtime cost
guideline: Prioritize algorithm and execution-path improvements in the code that dominates runtime cost to reduce baseline CPU and memory consumption where it matters most.
context: The framing here is about where effort pays off most: optimizing code that dominates runtime cost moves the baseline resource consumption meaningfully, while the same effort spent on rarely-executed code paths barely registers.

name: Cache responses that are repeated, predictable, or expensive to regenerate
guideline: Cache responses that are repeated, predictable, or expensive to regenerate, preventing recomputation of work that adds no value.
context: This is one of the concrete fixes to the chatty-API anti-pattern named elsewhere in this source: caching is what stops the same expensive computation from being repeated for what is effectively the same request.

name: Be cautious about adding abstraction in performance-critical paths
guideline: Be cautious about adding abstraction in performance-critical paths, since it limits execution overhead and coordination cost in hot paths.
context: Azure's specific caution: abstraction is generally good practice, but layered onto a performance-critical path it adds execution overhead and coordination cost exactly where that cost matters most — this isn't an argument against abstraction generally, just against it unexamined in hot paths.

name: Choose monolith or microservices based on real scaling and isolation needs
guideline: Choose monolith or microservices architecture based on real scaling and isolation needs, avoiding distributed-system overhead that doesn't improve outcomes.
context: This echoes the chatty-microservices anti-pattern described elsewhere in this source directly: choosing microservices because it's the more modern-sounding architecture, rather than because the workload genuinely has independent scaling or isolation needs, is exactly what introduces that unnecessary distributed-system overhead.

name: Evaluate SSR and CSR choices against their total compute and transfer footprint
guideline: Evaluate server-side versus client-side rendering choices against their total compute and transfer footprint to reduce redundant rendering and data movement.
context: Azure frames this as needing the full picture rather than a default preference: server-side rendering reduces client-device burden but adds server compute, while client-side rendering does the reverse — the actual total compute-plus-transfer footprint is what should decide it, not a blanket rule.

name: Remove cross-service data duplication and redundant domain models where possible
guideline: Remove cross-service data duplication and redundant domain models where possible to limit storage growth and compute amplification.
context: This is the storage-and-compute-amplification counterpart to the chatty-API problem named elsewhere in this source: the same data copied across multiple services' domain models costs both the extra storage and the extra compute of keeping every copy in sync.

name: Auto-scale workloads against observed demand rather than assumed peak usage
guideline: Auto-scale workloads against observed demand rather than assumed peak usage to reduce persistent overprovisioning and idle capacity.
context: Azure's framing: capacity is often sized for the peak load a team assumes might happen rather than what actually gets observed, which is exactly the gap between provisioned capacity and real demand that this pattern is meant to close.

name: Shut down or downsize non-production environments when they are not needed
guideline: Shut down or downsize non-production environments when they aren't needed to remove baseline consumption that delivers no business value.
context: Azure's concrete illustration: development and test environments often mirror production sizing while running at only a fraction of production's actual utilization — a mismatch that persists invisibly because the environment still appears healthy and working.

name: Remove orphaned and zombie resources on a regular cadence
guideline: Remove orphaned and zombie resources on a regular cadence to prevent silent cost accumulation from forgotten infrastructure.
context: The word Azure uses is "accumulation": this waste doesn't come from one bad decision but from forgotten infrastructure quietly piling up over time, which is why the guideline specifies a regular cadence rather than a one-time cleanup.

name: Match platform tiers and reservations to actual usage patterns
guideline: Match platform tiers and reservations to actual usage patterns to avoid paying for oversized infrastructure by default.
context: This is about a decision made once at setup and then left untouched: platform tier and reservation choices tend to get fixed early and rarely revisited even as actual usage patterns shift well away from what was originally provisioned for.

name: Favor containers, PaaS, or serverless when they fit the workload
guideline: Favor containers, PaaS, or serverless options when they fit the workload, improving utilization through more efficient shared platform capacity.
context: Azure's underlying reasoning: these options rely on shared platform capacity rather than infrastructure dedicated to one workload, so they tend to achieve better utilization by pooling demand across many tenants instead of each workload carrying its own idle headroom.

name: Use Spot VMs only where interruption is acceptable and recovery is understood
guideline: Use Spot VMs only where interruption is acceptable and recovery is well understood, using spare capacity efficiently without added operational risk.
context: The same tradeoff named for Spot VMs elsewhere in this source applies here from the cost angle too: spare capacity is genuinely cheaper to use, but only where the workload's tolerance for interruption and its recovery path are both well understood ahead of time.

name: Optimize CI/CD pipelines with caching, reuse, and incremental builds
guideline: Optimize CI/CD pipelines with caching, reuse, and incremental builds to cut redundant compute execution in engineering workflows.
context: Azure gives an explicit tradeoff here: caching reduces redundant compute execution, but it adds its own storage requirement and needs a cache-invalidation strategy — a poorly managed cache can produce stale build outputs, so the efficiency gain has to be balanced against that reliability risk.

name: Consider lower-carbon regions as part of workload placement decisions
guideline: Factor lower-carbon regions into workload placement decisions to reduce emissions per unit of compute when other requirements still hold.
context: Azure frames this as one factor among several, not an override: it's meant to be considered "as part of" placement decisions specifically when other requirements — compliance, latency, cost — still hold, not as the deciding factor on its own.

name: Schedule batch workloads to take advantage of lower-carbon or lower-cost periods
guideline: Schedule batch workloads to run during lower-carbon or lower-cost periods, aligning flexible compute with cleaner operating windows.
context: Azure's contrasting anti-pattern: batch processes that run on rigid, fixed schedules simply because that's operationally convenient, missing the opportunity to align with periods when the grid (or pricing) happens to be more favorable.

name: Place workloads closer to users when latency and transfer patterns justify it
guideline: Place workloads closer to users when latency and transfer patterns justify it, reducing network distance and unnecessary transfer cost.
context: This is scoped deliberately, not universal: Azure specifies "when latency and transfer patterns justify it," since moving a workload closer to users only pays off if enough of its traffic and data movement pattern actually depends on that proximity.

name: Avoid cross-region routing and replication that do not serve a clear workload need
guideline: Avoid cross-region routing and replication that don't serve a clear workload need, lowering network overhead and duplicated infrastructure activity.
context: Azure's illustrative anti-pattern: globally replicated deployments used by default even when actual demand is concentrated in a small set of regions, which introduces cross-region traffic and data movement that never gets used by real user demand.

name: Reassess regional deployment choices against actual usage over time
guideline: Periodically reassess regional deployment choices against actual usage to prevent static placement decisions from becoming long-term inefficiencies.
context: This closes the loop on regional placement decisions made elsewhere in this source: a region choice that was correct when user distribution and pricing looked one way can become a static, unexamined inefficiency once those conditions shift, which is why Azure frames this as a periodic reassessment rather than a one-time decision.

name: Use CDNs for content that is requested repeatedly at scale
guideline: Use CDNs for content requested repeatedly at scale to reduce origin compute demand and repeated network delivery.
context: Azure's framing: network cost is often underestimated because it's spread across many small interactions instead of concentrated in one obvious place — a CDN is specifically valuable for content requested at scale, where the same origin computation would otherwise repeat for every single request.

name: Compress payloads and choose transfer formats with care
guideline: Compress payloads and choose transfer formats carefully to lower bandwidth consumption without changing business outcomes.
context: This is scoped as "without changing business outcomes": the point is that compression and format choice are close to a pure efficiency win, with no functional tradeoff for the end user, unlike some of the other guidelines in this source that involve a genuine cost/benefit balance.

name: Reduce cross-service chaining and fan-out from a single user action
guideline: Reduce cross-service chaining and fan-out triggered by a single user action to prevent request amplification from multiplying backend work.
context: Azure's concrete illustration: a frontend that repeatedly fetches overlapping datasets across multiple components, where a single user action multiplies into several backend calls and repeated data transfers without actually improving what the user experiences.

name: Keep traffic within regional boundaries when the architecture allows it
guideline: Keep traffic within regional boundaries when the architecture allows it, avoiding expensive and unnecessary cross-region routing.
context: This is the network-level analogue to keeping dependent resources co-located: even when workloads are correctly placed near users, traffic that unnecessarily crosses regional boundaries mid-request still pays the cross-region routing cost this pattern is meant to avoid.

name: Place workloads near users when delivery patterns make that worthwhile
guideline: Place workloads near users when delivery patterns make it worthwhile, minimizing transfer distance and helping control latency-related overhead.
context: Distinct from the broader regional-placement guideline elsewhere in this source: this one is scoped specifically to delivery patterns — content and workloads whose value is mostly about proximity to where it's being consumed, rather than placement driven by compliance or cost.

name: Centralize media processing when the same transformations would otherwise be repeated
guideline: Centralize media processing when the same transformations would otherwise be repeated, reducing duplicated encoding and transformation work.
context: Azure's specific waste target: the same media transformation (resizing, transcoding, format conversion) being independently repeated by multiple services or requests, when centralizing that processing means it happens once and the result gets reused.

name: Match storage tiers to how often data is actually accessed
guideline: Match storage tiers to how often data is actually accessed to reduce infrastructure cost tied to over-served data.
context: Azure's framing is explicitly about avoidable cost: infrastructure cost "tied to over-served data" — keeping infrequently accessed data in a tier built for frequent access is paying for a capability that specific data doesn't actually need.

name: Remove stale, redundant, or low-value data on purpose
guideline: Actively remove stale, redundant, or low-value data to lower the long-term storage footprint without reducing useful capability.
context: The specific dynamic Azure names for storage broadly: deletion requires deliberate effort while retention is passive, so storage tends to grow regardless of actual business value unless someone actively works against that default.

name: Control logging and telemetry growth before retention becomes passive sprawl
guideline: Control logging and telemetry growth before retention becomes passive sprawl, preventing ingestion and storage costs from outpacing their value.
context: This is the storage-side counterpart to treating observability spend as part of the optimization scope (a related guideline): logs and telemetry are exactly the kind of data that accumulates passively and becomes "sprawl" if nobody is actively managing its retention.

name: Avoid duplicating datasets across services unless there is a clear reason
guideline: Avoid duplicating datasets across services unless there's a clear reason, reducing storage growth and repeated processing of the same data.
context: Azure frames the usual justification — convenience — directly: the same dataset gets copied across services or pipelines because it's easier than coordinating shared access, which is precisely the kind of "clear reason" this guideline asks you to require before duplicating.

name: Review backup retention policies against actual recovery requirements
guideline: Review backup retention policies against actual recovery requirements to eliminate redundant long-term storage that doesn't improve resilience.
context: Azure's framing: unmanaged backup recovery points can "silently accumulate" over time, growing storage footprint without a proportional increase in actual resilience — the fix is reviewing retention against what recovery genuinely requires, not against what's simply been kept by default.

name: Compress stored data where the tradeoff is favorable
guideline: Compress stored data where the tradeoff is favorable to reduce storage footprint and transfer volume with limited downside.
context: The qualifier "where the tradeoff is favorable" matters here: compression reduces storage footprint but costs compute to compress and decompress, so this is explicitly conditional rather than a blanket recommendation to compress everything.

name: Scale CI/CD resources dynamically instead of keeping capacity always available
guideline: Scale CI/CD resources dynamically instead of keeping capacity always available, preventing idle compute waste between engineering events.
context: Azure's framing: CI/CD capacity that's kept always-available regardless of actual pipeline activity is idle compute sitting between engineering events — the fix is scaling that capacity to match when builds and tests are actually running, not provisioning for constant readiness.

name: Cache build artifacts aggressively where reuse is reliable
guideline: Cache build artifacts aggressively where reuse is reliable to avoid repeated computation for unchanged inputs.
context: This directly targets a named anti-pattern in this source: pipelines treated as fixed workflows that rebuild everything from scratch even when the relevant inputs haven't actually changed since the last run.

name: Run tests for changed components when full-suite execution is not necessary
guideline: Run tests only for changed components when full-suite execution isn't necessary, reducing compute spent on validation that adds little signal.
context: Azure frames this in terms of signal, not just speed: full-suite execution on every change adds compute cost while often "adding little signal" beyond what testing just the changed components would already reveal.

name: Introduce incremental build strategies where tooling supports them well
guideline: Introduce incremental build strategies where tooling supports them well, limiting unnecessary full-system recomputation.
context: This is the build-side counterpart to targeted test execution named elsewhere in this source: rebuilding the whole system when only a small part changed is the same kind of unnecessary full-system recomputation, just at the build step rather than the test step.

name: Remove redundant pipeline stages and duplicate checks
guideline: Remove redundant pipeline stages and duplicate checks to lower the total compute footprint of delivery workflows.
context: Azure frames pipelines as accumulating redundancy over time much like storage does: stages and checks get added incrementally as the pipeline evolves, and without periodic review, duplicate or overlapping checks tend to persist even once they stop adding distinct value.

name: Avoid always-on full-suite testing when risk does not justify it
guideline: Avoid always-on full-suite testing when the risk doesn't justify it, reducing baseline CI/CD cost without losing meaningful validation.
context: This is the summary practice tying together the CI/CD guidelines in this source: matching testing intensity to actual risk, rather than running the maximum validation on every single change regardless of how much risk that particular change actually carries.

name: Establish a baseline of current carbon emissions for all workloads and services
guideline: Establish a baseline of current carbon emissions across workloads and services to provide a reference point for measuring improvement over time.
context: Azure frames this as the prerequisite for everything else in this section: without an established emissions baseline, later claims about carbon reduction have nothing concrete to measure improvement against.

name: Use emissions monitoring tools such as the Azure Carbon Optimizer to track environmental impact
guideline: Use emissions monitoring tools such as the Azure Carbon Optimizer to enable data-driven decisions and identify the largest sources of emissions.
context: Azure names its own concrete tool for this: the Azure Carbon Optimizer, which is presented as the practical way to get the data-driven visibility needed to identify the largest sources of emissions rather than estimating them indirectly.

name: Define carbon reduction targets for the workload and individual workload components
guideline: Define carbon reduction targets for the workload and its individual components to create clear objectives and drive accountability.
context: Azure specifies this at two levels: targets for the workload overall and for its individual components separately, so accountability for a reduction goal can be traced to the specific part of the system responsible rather than only tracked in aggregate.

name: Track sustainability using a combination of factors and a measurable metric such as an SCI score
guideline: Track sustainability through a combination of performance, carbon emissions, and cost proxies, developing a measurable metric (such as a Software Carbon Intensity score) and SLOs/SLAs to give a holistic view of workload efficiency.
context: Azure specifically names the Software Carbon Intensity (SCI) score — maintained by the Green Software Foundation — as a measurable metric to adopt here, tracked alongside existing SLOs and SLAs so carbon sits next to the performance indicators a team already reports on.

name: Record and assess the impact of all sustainability-related changes and optimizations
guideline: Record and assess the impact of every sustainability-related change to build an evidence-based view of the most effective reduction strategies.
context: This is what turns sustainability optimization from guesswork into an evidence-based practice: without recording the before/after impact of each change, it's hard to tell which optimizations are actually working and which just sounded reasonable.

name: Follow organizational governance to enforce sustainability outcomes in workload teams
guideline: Follow organizational governance to enforce sustainability outcomes across workload teams, establishing consistent practices and reducing variability.
context: Azure's stated risk if this is skipped: sustainability objectives "applied inconsistently across workloads, subscriptions, and teams" — governance is what turns a good intention into something reliably applied everywhere rather than only where an individual team happens to care.

name: Use existing cost governance controls and policies as part of sustainability initiatives
guideline: Reuse existing cost governance controls and policies as part of sustainability initiatives to reduce unnecessary resource consumption and lower emissions.
context: The practical efficiency here is about not duplicating effort: cost governance already targets oversized and underutilized resources for financial reasons, and that same enforcement mechanism reduces the associated emissions as a direct side effect.

name: Utilize built-in Azure Policy controls to enforce efficient resource configurations and operational standards
guideline: Use built-in Azure Policy controls to enforce efficient resource configurations and operational standards, promoting ongoing cloud efficiency.
context: Azure gives concrete examples of what policy-based controls can enforce: restricting oversized resources, requiring lifecycle management, mandating tags for sustainability reporting, blocking non-approved architectures, and steering toward efficient service selections.

name: Create a dedicated sustainability-focused Azure Policy initiative
guideline: Create a dedicated sustainability-focused Azure Policy initiative to embed sustainability into workload design, deployment, and operations.
context: Azure's specific suggestion: create a distinct Azure Policy initiative named for sustainability specifically, rather than folding sustainability rules loosely into existing general-purpose policy sets where they're easy to overlook or deprioritize.

name: Implement data lifecycle management policies to ensure only necessary data is collected, retained, and processed
guideline: Implement data lifecycle management policies (for example, using Microsoft Purview for classification and retention, and Azure Monitor Data Collection Rules to control telemetry) so only necessary data is collected and retained, reducing storage, transfer, and processing overhead.
context: Azure names two concrete tools for this: Microsoft Purview to classify data and apply retention rules that automatically delete it after a defined period, and Azure Monitor Data Collection Rules to control what telemetry actually gets collected, transformed, and routed in the first place.

name: Regularly review policy compliance and identify opportunities for further optimization
guideline: Regularly review policy compliance and look for further optimization opportunities to sustain long-term efficiency gains.
context: This closes the loop on the policy-based controls named elsewhere in this source: policies only stay effective if compliance against them gets checked regularly, rather than assumed to hold once they're initially put in place.

name: Establish a sustainability community or center of excellence responsible for promoting cloud efficiency and green software practices
guideline: Establish a sustainability community or center of excellence to create organizational ownership and consistently drive green software practices.
context: Azure's named risk if this doesn't exist: sustainability knowledge and accountability concentrated in a small group of specialists, where valuable lessons and successful practices stay isolated within individual teams instead of spreading across the organization.

name: Provide ongoing sustainability and green software training for architects, developers, and operations teams
guideline: Provide ongoing sustainability and green software training for architects, developers, and operations teams to improve environmentally responsible decision-making.
context: Azure scopes this across three distinct roles rather than one generic training: architects, developers, and operations teams each make different day-to-day decisions that affect sustainability, so each needs training relevant to their own specific decisions.

name: Define sustainability policies, targets, and expectations, and communicate them regularly across the organization
guideline: Define sustainability policies, targets, and expectations, and communicate them regularly to align teams around common objectives.
context: Azure's stated risk if sustainability goals aren't clearly communicated and measured: they get perceived as secondary to other business priorities, and end up inconsistently incorporated into planning and design decisions over time.

name: Create a centralized repository for sustainability guidance, best practices, and lessons learned
guideline: Create a centralized repository of sustainability guidance and lessons learned to accelerate adoption and reduce duplicated effort.
context: The efficiency case here is specifically about avoiding duplicated effort: without a shared repository, different teams tend to independently rediscover the same optimization approaches rather than building on what another team already learned.

name: Encourage regular knowledge-sharing sessions, workshops, or internal webinars focused on sustainability
guideline: Encourage regular knowledge-sharing sessions or webinars on sustainability to promote continuous learning and scale successful initiatives.
context: This is the recurring, ongoing counterpart to the one-time training guideline elsewhere in this source: sustainability practice evolves, so continuous knowledge-sharing is what keeps successful initiatives spreading across teams rather than staying confined to wherever they originated.

name: Include sustainability metrics and objectives as part of workload governance, performance reviews, or KPIs
guideline: Include sustainability metrics and objectives in workload governance, performance reviews, or KPIs to embed them into decision-making.
context: Azure's framing: folding sustainability into performance reviews and KPIs is what embeds it into actual decision-making, as opposed to being tracked on a separate dashboard that influences nothing about how teams are actually evaluated.

name: Recognize and reward teams that achieve sustainability goals through incentives, gamification, or certifications
guideline: Recognize and reward teams that achieve sustainability goals through incentives, gamification, or certifications to encourage continued participation.
context: Azure names specific mechanisms for this: incentives, gamification, and formal sustainability certifications or badges — concrete recognition rather than a generic acknowledgment, meant to actively encourage continued participation rather than just applaud a single achievement.

name: Promote carbon-aware and carbon-optimized application design practices across all workload teams
guideline: Promote carbon-aware and carbon-optimized application design practices across all workload teams to reduce emissions over time.
context: This is the summary practice for the whole Operational Excellence section: baselines, targets, governance, and training all ultimately exist to support carbon-aware design decisions becoming standard practice across every workload team, not just the ones that started the initiative.

name: Optimize API communication patterns by reducing chatty interactions, minimizing payload sizes, and using efficient message encoding techniques
guideline: Optimize API communication by reducing chatty interactions, minimizing payload size, and using efficient encoding to cut network traffic and energy use.
context: Azure points to its own documented feature for this specifically: "Environmentally sustainable APIs in Azure API Management," treating efficient API design as something the platform itself has built-in support for rather than purely an application-level discipline.

name: Implement request throttling and response caching by using services such as Azure API Management
guideline: Implement request throttling and response caching (for example with Azure API Management) to prevent unnecessary and repeated backend processing.
context: Azure API Management is named as the concrete service for this — the same platform referenced for sustainable API design elsewhere in this source, now specifically for its request-throttling and response-caching capabilities.

name: Monitor API usage patterns and continuously optimize high-volume or inefficient endpoints
guideline: Monitor API usage patterns and continuously optimize high-volume or inefficient endpoints to reduce resource utilization and carbon footprint.
context: This is meant as an ongoing practice rather than a one-time audit: usage patterns shift as an application evolves, so a previously-efficient endpoint can become the highest-volume or least-efficient one over time without anyone noticing unless it's actively monitored.

name: Evaluate rendering strategies and select server-side or client-side rendering based on user device capabilities, network conditions, and workload requirements
guideline: Choose server-side or client-side rendering based on device capabilities, network conditions, and workload needs to optimize compute utilization across client and server.
context: Azure lays out the actual tradeoff rather than favoring one approach: server-side rendering shifts processing burden off end-user devices and benefits from centralized caching and efficient infrastructure, while client-side rendering shifts load off the server and can take advantage of modern device capabilities and browser caching instead.

name: Leverage caching mechanisms, whether centralized on the server or within the browser, to minimize repeated rendering and data processing operations
guideline: Use server-side or browser caching to minimize repeated rendering and data processing, reducing compute and network resource use.
context: This is the concrete mechanism that makes the SSR-vs-CSR choice less costly either way: whichever rendering strategy is chosen, caching is what prevents the same rendering or data-processing work from being repeated for requests that would produce an identical result.

name: Design lightweight and efficient user interfaces by minimizing unnecessary components, pages, and media assets
guideline: Design lightweight, efficient user interfaces with minimal unnecessary components and media assets to reduce network traffic and compute use.
context: Azure frames UI design choices as having "a significant impact" on sustainability specifically: complex interfaces, large media assets, and excessive page content all increase network traffic and processing on both the client and server side, not just one or the other.

name: Optimize content delivery by using appropriately sized images and videos, avoiding unnecessary asset downloads, and leveraging system fonts where practical
guideline: Optimize content delivery with appropriately sized media, avoid unnecessary asset downloads, and use system fonts where practical to lower bandwidth and client-side processing.
context: This is one of the concrete techniques behind the broader lightweight-UI guideline named elsewhere in this source — appropriately sized images/videos and system fonts specifically target bandwidth and client-side processing rather than the interface's structural complexity.

name: Improve user navigation and findability, and consider offering resource-efficient experiences such as simplified interfaces or dark mode options
guideline: Improve navigation and findability, and consider resource-efficient experiences such as simplified interfaces or dark mode, to reduce unnecessary data retrieval and energy use.
context: Azure frames the user-experience angle specifically here: better navigation reduces the number of page loads and data retrievals a user needs to accomplish a task, while options like dark mode are named as resource-efficient experience choices in their own right.

name: Profile workloads to understand concurrency patterns, resource utilization, and opportunities for performance optimization or parallelization
guideline: Profile workloads to understand concurrency and resource utilization, uncovering opportunities for optimization or parallelization that improve compute efficiency.
context: Azure's stated risk if this step is skipped: without measuring how an application actually consumes CPU, memory, and processing capacity, a team "might unknowingly deploy inefficient code or underutilize available infrastructure" without ever finding out.

name: Evaluate specialized compute options, such as GPU-based resources, where they provide efficiency gains
guideline: Evaluate specialized compute options such as GPUs where they provide genuine efficiency gains, balancing performance benefit against higher operational cost.
context: Azure names an explicit tradeoff here: GPU-based resources can meaningfully improve efficiency for machine learning and highly parallel workloads, but they typically cost more to operate than CPU-based alternatives — the recommendation is to verify the performance benefit actually justifies that added expense, not to default to GPUs generally.

name: Establish CPU and memory baselines and incorporate sustainability-focused testing, monitoring, alerts, and quality gates into deployment pipelines
guideline: Establish CPU and memory baselines and build sustainability-focused testing, monitoring, and quality gates into deployment pipelines to catch inefficient code before production.
context: Azure's stated purpose: catching inefficient code and excessive resource consumption before it reaches production, using quality gates the same way a team would gate on test coverage or security scanning — inefficiency becomes something a deployment pipeline can actually block, not just something noticed after the fact.

name: Use content delivery networks (CDNs), caching strategies, including in-memory caching where appropriate, and data compression techniques to reduce network traffic and optimize content delivery
guideline: Use CDNs, caching strategies (including in-memory caching), and data compression to reduce network traffic and optimize content delivery.
context: Azure names an explicit tradeoff for this whole category: caching and compression genuinely reduce bandwidth, but they can require additional compute, memory, or storage resources of their own — tuning retention and compression strategy is about balancing those two costs against each other, not assuming the network savings are free.

name: Deploy workloads and content closer to users and keep dependent resources within the same cloud and region where practical
guideline: Deploy workloads and content closer to users and keep dependent resources within the same cloud and region where practical, minimizing network traversal.
context: Azure's framing goes beyond just latency: keeping dependent resources within the same cloud and region also reduces reliance on public internet routing specifically, which is a distinct source of unpredictability and overhead beyond the raw distance data has to travel.

name: Regularly review and tune caching configurations, such as cache retention and expiration settings, to maximize efficiency and resource utilization
guideline: Regularly review and tune caching configurations, such as retention and expiration settings, to maximize cache effectiveness and reduce unnecessary data transfer.
context: This is the maintenance counterpart to setting up caching in the first place: retention and expiration settings that were reasonable when configured can become stale as access patterns shift, so this needs periodic re-tuning rather than a one-time setup.

name: Apply storage compression, optimize database queries, and reduce unnecessary data transfer to improve storage efficiency and performance
